title: LU decomposition
summary: LU writes A as a unit lower-triangular L times an upper-triangular U. It exists with no row swap when every leading principal minor is nonzero. With partial pivoting the factorization is PA=LU, and not every invertible matrix factors without a swap.
intuition:
LU factorization is Gaussian elimination stored as two triangular matrices. The upper factor $U$ is the row echelon matrix the elimination produces, pivots and all. The lower factor $L$ stores the multipliers, with ones on its diagonal: if row $i$ was replaced by row $i$ minus $\ell_{ij}$ times pivot row $j$, that multiplier $\ell_{ij}$ is the $(i,j)$ entry of $L$. The convention in this lesson is that $L$ is unit lower triangular, so the pivots sit in $U$, not in $L$. Multiplying $LU$ undoes the bookkeeping and returns $A$, provided no row was swapped.

No-swap elimination finishes with a nonzero pivot in every column exactly when every leading principal minor of $A$ is nonzero. The $k$-th pivot equals $\Delta_k/\Delta_{k-1}$, with $\Delta_0=1$ and $\Delta_k$ the $k$-th leading principal minor. So the algorithm meets only nonzero pivots if and only if those minors are all nonzero, and in that case $A=LU$ with this unit $L$. The condition is sufficient for the factorization. It is the right hypothesis to quote. It is not true of every invertible matrix.

A row exchange is sometimes required even when $A$ is invertible. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-1$ and leading principal minor $0$. Suppose $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\a&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\0&r\end{pmatrix}$. The product has top-left entry $p$, so $p=0$, and then the bottom-left entry $ap$ cannot equal $1$. There is no LU factorization. Partial pivoting swaps the rows first. With a permutation matrix $P$ recording the swaps, the factored equation is $PA=LU$. Every invertible matrix has a factorization of that form. The version without $P$ is the special case $P=I$.

definitions.body: An LU factorization is $A=LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal, zeros above) and $U$ upper triangular. The entries of $L$ below the diagonal are the elimination multipliers.

The $k$-th leading principal minor $\Delta_k$ is the determinant of the top-left $k\times k$ corner of $A$. If every $\Delta_k$ is nonzero, then $A=LU$ exists with no row swap, and the $k$-th pivot is $\Delta_k/\Delta_{k-1}$.
With partial pivoting, the factorization is $PA=LU$, where $P$ is the permutation matrix of the row swaps. Not every invertible matrix has an LU factorization with $P=I$.

formulas.name: LU
formulas.note: $L$ is unit lower triangular and $U$ is upper. This form, with no row swap, exists when every leading principal minor is nonzero, equivalently when every pivot the algorithm encounters is nonzero.

formulas.name: With row swaps
formulas.note: $P$ is a permutation matrix from partial pivoting. Do not drop $P$: an invertible matrix need not have an LU factorization without row exchanges.

properties: $L$ has ones on the diagonal. The pivots are the diagonal entries of $U$, not of $L$.
If every leading principal minor is nonzero, then $A=LU$ with unit lower-triangular $L$ and upper-triangular $U$, and no row swap is required.
For the algorithm, that minor condition is equivalent to every pivot encountered being nonzero. The $k$-th pivot equals $\Delta_k/\Delta_{k-1}$.
With partial pivoting the stored factorization is $PA=LU$. Row swaps are part of the statement.
Not every invertible matrix satisfies $A=LU$ without a permutation. $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible and has no such factorization.

examples.title: A $3\times 3$ factorization, multiplied back
examples.prompt: Factor $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&3&3\\2&1&2\end{pmatrix}$ as $LU$ with unit lower-triangular $L$, and multiply $LU$ to recover $A$.
steps: The leading minors are $\Delta_1=2$, $\Delta_2=\det\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\4&3\end{pmatrix}=2$, and $\Delta_3=\det A=2$, all nonzero, so no swap is required. The multipliers are $\ell_{21}=4/2=2$ and $\ell_{31}=2/2=1$. After those subtractions the $(3,2)$ entry is already $0$, so $\ell_{32}=0$.
Thus $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. The pivots $2,1,1$ match $\Delta_1$, $\Delta_2/\Delta_1$, and $\Delta_3/\Delta_2$.

examples.title: An invertible matrix with no LU factorization
examples.prompt: Show that $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has no factorization $A=LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper triangular. Give a $PA=LU$ factorization instead.
steps: The leading principal minor is $0$, so the no-pivot algorithm stops at once. Suppose toward a contradiction that $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\a&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\0&r\end{pmatrix}$. Then $LU=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\ap&aq+r\end{pmatrix}$.
Matching $A$ forces $p=0$ and $q=1$, and then the bottom-left entry $ap=0$ cannot equal $1$. No such factors exist, even though $\det A=-1$ and $A$ is invertible.
Swap the two rows: $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $PA=I$. Then $PA=LU$ with $L=I$ and $U=I$. The permutation is essential.
examples.answer: There is no $A=LU$ of the required shape. After the swap, $PA=I$ is an LU factorization with $L=U=I$.

traps: Claiming every invertible matrix has an LU factorization with no row exchange. $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a counterexample: the $(1,1)$ entry of $LU$ would have to be both a pivot and zero.
Putting the pivots on the diagonal of $L$. In this convention $L$ is unit lower triangular, with ones on the diagonal, and the pivots are the diagonal of $U$.

Forgetting to multiply by $P$ when a swap happened. The multipliers from a pivoted elimination rebuild $PA$, not $A$, unless you also move the rows of $L$ in the matching way. The safe statement is $PA=LU$.

Treating a zero leading minor as a rounding nuisance that the same formulas survive. A zero $\Delta_k$ means a zero pivot. The factorization without a swap is then not the one this algorithm produces.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

def det2(M):
    return M[0][0] * M[1][1] - M[0][1] * M[1][0]

A = [[2, 1, 1], [4, 3, 3], [2, 1, 2]]
L = [[1, 0, 0], [2, 1, 0], [1, 0, 1]]
U = [[2, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1]]
assert mul(L, U) == A
assert det2([[2, 1], [4, 3]]) == 2
# no LU for the swap matrix: p would be 0 and a*p would need to be 1
Bad = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]
assert Bad[0][0] == 0
assert det2(Bad) == -1
P = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]
assert mul(P, Bad) == [[1, 0], [0, 1]]
print(2)

questions.stem: In the factorization $A=LU$ used in this lesson, the factor $L$ is
options: upper triangular with ones on the diagonal
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. The convention is that $L$ is unit lower triangular: ones on the diagonal and the multipliers below it. The factor $U$ is upper triangular and carries the pivots. Orthogonality and symmetry are different factorizations.

questions.stem: After partial pivoting, the LU factorization of a square matrix is written
options: $A=LU$ with no permutation, for every invertible $A$
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. Partial pivoting records its row swaps in a permutation matrix $P$, and the triangular factors then satisfy $PA=LU$. Option A is false: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible and has no unpermuted LU factorization. The other two options are the SVD and the symmetric spectral theorem.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: If every leading principal minor of $A$ is nonzero, then $A=LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper, and no row swap is required.
Every invertible matrix has an LU factorization with no row exchange.
$\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has no LU factorization with unit lower-triangular $L$.
The no-pivoting algorithm produces $A=LU$ when every pivot it encounters is nonzero.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, C, and D**. Nonzero leading minors are equivalent to nonzero pivots in the algorithm, and either condition produces $A=LU$ with unit $L$. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has first leading minor $0$ and cannot be written $LU$: the top-left entry of any such product would be the first pivot, which would have to be $0$ and $1$ at once. Invertibility does not remove the need for a possible row swap.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&3&3\\2&1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and $U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. Row $2$ of $LU$ is $2(2,1,1)+(0,1,1)=(4,3,3)$, and row $3$ is $(2,1,1)+(0,0,1)=(2,1,2)$, so the product is $A$. The diagonal of $L$ is $(1,1,1)$ and $U$ has zeros below the diagonal. The determinant equals the product of the pivots $2\cdot 1\cdot 1=2$, not $0$.

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&3&3\\2&1&2\end{pmatrix}=LU$ with the unit lower-triangular $L$ from elimination without row swaps, enter the product of the diagonal entries of $U$.
questions.solution: The answer is **2**. Elimination produces $U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so the diagonal product is $2\cdot 1\cdot 1=2$. Because $L$ has unit diagonal and no row was swapped, this product is also $\det A$.
